paragraphs: Recognizing a new class from only a few examples is difficult because those examples can give a distorted picture of the class. Distribution calibration addresses this by borrowing statistical information from familiar classes with abundant data. This paper focuses on deciding how much information to borrow from each familiar class, rather than treating those transfer weights as a secondary design choice.

The proposed method learns these weights through two levels of optimal transport. At the higher level, it matches novel samples with base classes; the resulting transport plan supplies the weights for transferring statistics. The lower level determines the matching costs by considering the weighted samples within each base class. This lets the transfer decision account for the data underlying a class.

Experiments on standard benchmarks report better performance than competing approaches and favorable generalization across domains. The findings support adaptive weighting as a useful component of distribution calibration. The method is presented as a plug-and-play addition, making the contribution a way to improve few-shot learning through better use of existing class information.
neurips-2022-adaptive-distribution-calib.tldr: A hierarchical optimal transport method learns how much statistical information to transfer from familiar classes to new classes with few examples.

paragraphs: Coordinating many agents becomes difficult when every agent must consider everything happening in an environment. ALMA addresses tasks that have a useful structure: they consist of local subtasks, and an agent can meaningfully concentrate on one assigned subtask. For these composite tasks, coordination can be separated into deciding who works where and deciding how each agent should act.

ALMA learns both levels together. A high-level policy allocates agents to subtasks, while low-level policies guide their actions within those assignments. This structure reduces what individual agents need to observe and encourages reuse of subtask policies across different combinations of work. A new combination can therefore benefit from behaviors learned for its constituent subtasks.

Across challenging environments, the authors report sophisticated coordination, stronger performance than strong baselines, and better generalization to new configurations. They also examine combining allocation and action policies trained separately. Although ALMA supports that combination, joint training produces the best reported performance, indicating that allocation decisions and local behaviors benefit from adapting to one another.
neurips-2022-alma-hierarchical-learning-.tldr: ALMA jointly learns subtask assignments and local agent behaviors to improve coordination and generalization in composite multi-agent tasks.

paragraphs: Researchers study performance on unfamiliar data through several different targets, including confidence calibration, resistance to adversarial attacks, and robustness to artificial corruptions. These targets share a broad motivation, but they can lead to different recommendations. This paper asks what happens when those research directions are evaluated under common experimental conditions using real data.

The study collects 172 publicly available dataset pairs for training and evaluation outside the training distribution. It fine-tunes more than 31,000 networks drawn from nine architectures, covering settings with both many and few examples. The evaluation includes accuracy, calibration error, adversarial attacks, environment invariance, and synthetic corruptions, bringing multiple notions of robustness into one investigation.

The results confirm a tendency for accuracy on familiar and unfamiliar distributions to improve together. However, the relationship depends strongly on the dataset and is more complicated than earlier, smaller studies suggested. The practical implication is that improvements in ordinary accuracy are informative, but the evidence does not support a single dataset-independent relationship describing performance under distribution shifts.
neurips-2022-assaying-out-of-distributio.tldr: A large transfer-learning study finds that familiar-data and shifted-data accuracy often improve together, but their relationship depends strongly on the dataset.

paragraphs: Discovering governing equations from measurements can make a dynamical system easier to understand and predict. Sparse observations and substantial noise make that task difficult, especially when the goal includes quantifying uncertainty. This paper develops a Bayesian spline framework that seeks compact equations for dynamics evolving over time or across both space and time.

Splines provide a representation of the measurements from which derivatives can be computed and used to build candidate equation terms. Learning also uses equation residuals, so the proposed dynamics help inform the spline representation. Approximate Bayesian techniques estimate posterior distributions over trainable parameters, attaching uncertainty to the learned system rather than returning only a single fitted description.

To favor concise equations, the method iteratively thresholds terms within a Bayesian learning procedure and uses alternating optimization to approximate a constraint on the number of retained terms. Evaluations cover nonlinear systems governed by ordinary and partial differential equations. Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate the approach's reported advantages in these settings, supporting the combination of data fitting, equation discovery, and uncertainty estimation.
neurips-2022-bayesian-spline-learning-fo.tldr: Bayesian spline learning discovers compact nonlinear governing equations from sparse, noisy measurements while estimating uncertainty in the learned system.

paragraphs: Certifying that a function is convex helps establish useful structure for optimization. The Hessian, which describes second-order curvature, provides a natural route: its positive semidefiniteness is the relevant property to check. The practical challenge is representing and analyzing that Hessian automatically for functions used in machine learning.

This paper builds on a way to compute computational graphs for Hessians within a function class broad enough to support classical machine learning. It introduces a method for checking these graphs for positive semidefiniteness. The resulting system turns curvature information into a computational certificate rather than requiring a separate manual argument for each function.

The authors compare this approach with disciplined convex programming, an established method for recognizing convex expressions. They prove that their Hessian approach is at least as powerful for differentiable functions. Against a state-of-the-art DCP implementation, it can certify a larger class of differentiable functions. This is a claim about the reach of the certification method, not a claim that every convex function can be recognized.
neurips-2022-convexity-certificates-from.tldr: Checking computational graphs of Hessians yields convexity certificates that match DCP's power for differentiable functions and exceed a leading implementation.

paragraphs: Consistency and coherence are important goals for neural reasoning, yet evaluating them requires precise definitions. Symbolic systems already provide formal ways to discuss these properties, while neural systems have lacked equivalent foundations. This paper introduces formal definitions intended to provide a common basis for quantitative evaluation and comparison across neural, neuro-symbolic, and transfer-learning approaches.

The authors put those definitions to work by designing a dynamic relation-decoder model around them. Rather than leaving the contribution at the level of terminology, they use the proposed principles to guide a concrete model. They also introduce a dataset and compare the model with existing relation decoders on a partial transfer-learning task.

The experiments show that decoders maintaining consistency in unobserved parts of representation space retain coherence across domains and achieve better transfer performance. This connects properties of the learned representation beyond observed examples with behavior in another domain. The reported connection is experimental: it illustrates the usefulness of the definitions and model without establishing that consistency alone universally guarantees successful transfer.
neurips-2022-formalizing-consistency-and.tldr: Formal definitions of neural consistency and coherence guide a relation decoder whose experiments connect these properties with improved transfer learning.

paragraphs: Text rationalization tries to explain a prediction by selecting meaningful portions of the input. A common design uses a generator to select text and a predictor to make a decision from that selection. This arrangement can create a harmful feedback loop: an immature generator produces noisy selections, the predictor overfits to them, and its feedback encourages the generator to keep selecting unhelpful text.

Folded Rationalization addresses this interaction by sharing an encoder between the generator and predictor. The two roles use a unified mechanism for extracting text meaning. This gives the predictor access to valuable information that a conventional generator can block, with the aim of improving the predictor and, through it, the generator.

The authors report empirical F1 improvements of up to 10.3% compared with state-of-the-art methods. That figure describes the largest stated improvement, rather than an improvement guaranteed in every setting. The broader contribution is an architectural response to degeneration: improving how the selection and prediction components share information can improve the quality of rationalization.
neurips-2022-fr-folded-rationalization-w.tldr: Folded Rationalization shares an encoder between text selection and prediction to reduce degeneration, reporting F1 improvements of up to 10.3%.

paragraphs: A learned fluid simulator needs to capture complex motion while respecting physical structure. This paper makes conservation of linear momentum a hard constraint in the model. It implements that constraint through antisymmetrical continuous convolutional layers, building a specific conservation law into the simulator's architecture.

The conservation mechanism is combined with a hierarchical network, a carefully designed resampling scheme, and training that promotes temporal coherence. These components address the simulator as an evolving system, where accuracy depends on more than an isolated prediction. Together, they substantially improve physical accuracy in the reported evaluations. The imposed physical structure also provides a bias that helps the model generalize.

Tests span several challenging fluid scenarios, including new scenarios containing up to one million particles. The authors report stronger generalization and training performance than existing approaches, along with greater reliability on unseen cases. The hard guarantee concerns linear momentum conservation; the broader gains in accuracy and generalization are demonstrated experimentally. This distinction separates a property enforced by construction from the model's measured behavior.
neurips-2022-guaranteed-conservation-of-.tldr: A fluid simulator enforces linear momentum conservation architecturally and demonstrates improved accuracy and generalization, including scenarios with one million particles.

paragraphs: Two neural networks may produce different internal representations, but the practical importance of that difference depends on what predictions those representations support. GULP introduces a family of distances motivated explicitly by downstream prediction. Its goal is to make representation comparison informative about how useful the features are for subsequent learning.

By construction, the distance uniformly controls differences in prediction performance for regularized linear prediction tasks. This gives the comparison a defined predictive scope. GULP also satisfies the triangle inequality and remains unchanged under orthogonal transformations, so rotating a representation does not by itself change the comparison. These properties make it suitable for embedding and visualizing relationships among representations.

The authors evaluate GULP against other comparison methods. They report that it distinguishes architecture families, converges as training proceeds, and captures generalization performance on downstream linear tasks. Together, the theoretical construction and experiments connect representational similarity to a concrete use of the features. The predictive guarantee specifically concerns regularized linear tasks, which is central to interpreting what the distance measures.
neurips-2022-gulp-a-prediction-based-met.tldr: GULP compares neural representations through distances that control performance differences on regularized linear prediction tasks.

paragraphs: ReLU networks represent continuous piecewise linear functions, and such functions can also be represented by these networks. The question is how many neurons an exact representation requires. Earlier upper bounds grew extremely quickly with the number of pieces or distinct linear components, making the apparent representation cost large.

This paper proves that a number of hidden neurons at most quadratic in the number of pieces is sufficient. That upper bound does not depend on input dimension. The authors also provide a polynomial-time algorithm for constructing a network meeting their bounds, so the result supplies both a size guarantee and a way to realize it.

When the number of distinct linear components is known as well, the bound becomes bilinear in the relevant counts, improving on the quadratic bound. If the piece count is unknown, bounds expressed through distinct components are polynomial for low-dimensional inputs and factorial in the worst case. These are sufficient representation sizes, not claims that every function requires that many neurons, and they substantially tighten previous guarantees.
neurips-2022-improved-bounds-on-neural-c.tldr: Any continuous piecewise linear function has an exact ReLU representation with at most quadratically many hidden neurons in its piece count, independent of input dimension.

paragraphs: Insertion-based text generation builds an output by inserting text into an evolving context. Many existing approaches repeatedly encode that context after each insertion, making training expensive. InsNet introduces a position encoding designed around insertion operations so that computation can be shared across the training sequence.

With this encoding, training needs only one context-encoding pass for the entire insertion sequence. InsNet also offers a controllable choice between parallel and sequential decoding. This allows it to accommodate tasks with different opportunities for parallel generation: machine translation can benefit from parallelism, while generation constrained to include specified words can use a more sequential process to support output quality.

The evaluation covers two datasets for unsupervised lexically constrained generation and three for machine translation. The authors report advantages over earlier insertion-based methods in training speed, inference efficiency, and generation quality. The contribution therefore combines more efficient training with flexibility at generation time, addressing both repeated computation and the need to adapt decoding behavior to the task.
neurips-2022-insnet-an-efficient-flexibl.tldr: InsNet shares context computation during insertion-based training and supports both parallel and sequential decoding, improving reported efficiency and generation quality.

paragraphs: Singing voice synthesis depends on recordings paired with accurate musical information. A shortage of public, high-quality, carefully labeled data has limited work in this area. M4Singer addresses that resource problem with a free-to-use Mandarin singing collection that includes multiple singers, styles, and manually prepared musical scores.

The corpus contains recordings by 20 professional singers covering 700 Chinese pop songs. It includes soprano, alto, tenor, and bass voices, providing coverage across all four SATB categories. The authors manually compose scores for each recorded song, supplying information needed to study prosody modeling in singing synthesis. The scores are thus a central part of the resource, alongside the audio recordings.

Four benchmark experiments demonstrate uses of the collection: score-based singing synthesis, controllable singing voice, singing voice conversion, and automatic music transcription. These tasks cover generating singing, controlling it, converting voices, and recovering musical information from audio. The paper's contribution is a shared dataset with accompanying benchmarks, intended to make several strands of singing research easier to develop and evaluate.
neurips-2022-m4singer-a-multi-style-mult.tldr: M4Singer provides Mandarin singing recordings from 20 professional singers across 700 songs, with manually prepared scores and four benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Training a control policy in simulation can avoid the cost and risk of real-world training, but a simulator may misrepresent the environment where the policy will operate. This paper studies that mismatch through uncertain simulation parameters and a specified set of possible parameter values. Its objective is strong performance in the worst case within that set.

The proposed M2TD3 algorithm uses an off-policy actor-critic approach to solve a max-min problem. Policy learning seeks to improve performance while the opposing optimization seeks unfavorable uncertainty parameters. Simultaneous gradient ascent and descent couple these two directions, making robustness to modeled uncertainty part of the training objective.

Experiments in MuJoCo environments show better worst-case performance than several baseline approaches. This supports the method's ability to handle the uncertainty considered in those evaluations. The scope of the robustness objective is the chosen parameter set: the motivation for real-world guarantees depends on that set representing the relevant mismatch. The reported evidence itself consists of comparative worst-case results in simulation environments.
neurips-2022-max-min-off-policy-actor-cr.tldr: M2TD3 trains policies against worst-case simulation parameters and achieves stronger worst-case performance than several baselines in MuJoCo experiments.

paragraphs: Online imitation learning uses expert demonstrations together with access to an environment or accurate simulator. Even when optimization is exact, a finite demonstration set introduces sampling variance that can leave a performance gap. This paper targets that statistical problem by improving the estimate of where the expert's behavior takes it.

Replay estimation repeatedly executes cached expert actions in a stochastic simulator. These replays produce a smoother estimate of the expert visitation distribution for the learner to match. With general function approximation, the authors prove a theorem connecting the resulting performance gap to parameter estimation error in an offline classification problem for learning the expert policy.

For tabular models and linear function approximation, the analysis achieves the optimal dependence, up to logarithmic factors, given by the smaller of H^(3/2)/N_exp and H/sqrt(N_exp). Here H is the horizon and N_exp is the expert dataset size. The assumptions are substantially weaker than in prior work. Implementations on continuous-control tasks also significantly improve policy performance across multiple dataset sizes, complementing the theoretical result.
neurips-2022-minimax-optimal-online-imit.tldr: Replaying expert actions in a stochastic simulator reduces estimation variance and yields optimal imitation-learning guarantees in tabular and linear settings.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models expand parameter capacity while activating only part of the model for each input. Their effectiveness depends on routing: uneven workloads can leave some experts poorly trained or poorly specialized. Conventional top-k routing assigns a fixed number of experts to every token, regardless of differences between tokens.

Expert choice reverses the assignment direction. Each expert selects its top-k tokens, giving the expert a fixed bucket size while allowing individual tokens to reach different numbers of experts. This changes how computation is distributed: expert workloads are controlled directly, and token coverage can vary instead of being fixed in advance.

Using the same computational resources as Switch Transformer top-1 and GShard top-2 routing, the method improves training convergence time by more than twofold. It also reports higher fine-tuning performance at equal computational cost across 11 selected GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks. At a smaller activation cost, it beats dense T5 on seven of those tasks. These comparisons support routing direction as an important efficiency and performance choice.
neurips-2022-mixture-of-experts-with-exp.tldr: Letting experts select tokens balances expert workloads and allows variable token coverage, with reported gains in training speed and downstream performance.

paragraphs: Generative neural networks can provide prior structure for recovering signals, but analyzing the reconstruction process is difficult. Earlier rigorous analysis of multi-layer approximate message passing relied on fully connected layers with independent Gaussian weights. That assumption leaves out convolutional structures that are common in practical generative priors.

This paper establishes state evolution for the algorithm when the generative layers are random convolutions. State evolution supplies a rigorous description of the reconstruction algorithm's behavior. The central result places these random convolutional layers in the same universality class as Gaussian matrices, extending the earlier theoretical framework to a different and practically relevant layer structure.

The proof constructs a connection between convolutional matrices and spatially coupled sensing matrices from coding theory. This connection is also presented as a contribution of independent interest, linking two kinds of structured inference problems. The result specifically concerns random convolutional designs; its significance is that rigorous analysis can accommodate convolutional structure without retaining the restrictive fully connected, independent-weight model.
neurips-2022-multi-layer-state-evolution.tldr: The paper extends rigorous state evolution for multi-layer approximate message passing to random convolutional layers through a connection with coding-theory matrices.

paragraphs: In stochastic games, players learn while responding both to one another and to an environment that changes over time. This makes policy-gradient convergence harder to understand than in some special game classes. The paper studies behavior near Nash equilibrium policies satisfying a second-order stationarity condition related to sufficient conditions in optimization.

The first result shows that these policies attract nearby learning trajectories with high probability. For policy gradients estimated using REINFORCE, the authors establish a squared-distance convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(n)) when the step size is selected appropriately. The result describes local convergence under the stated equilibrium and step-size conditions, rather than convergence from every possible starting policy.

For the more specialized class of deterministic Nash policies, the analysis gives a substantially stronger conclusion: policy-gradient methods converge in finitely many iterations. Together, these findings distinguish general local attraction from faster behavior in a particular policy class. They extend understanding of policy-gradient learning beyond the special classes of stochastic games where convergence had been better understood.
neurips-2022-on-the-convergence-of-polic.tldr: Policy gradients locally approach second-order stationary Nash policies with high probability, with finite-iteration convergence in the studied deterministic-policy case.

paragraphs: Point-cloud registration aligns two collections of 3D points, which may initially use different reference frames. Position information is important for Transformer-based registration, but raw coordinates can be difficult to compare across those frames. This paper proposes a positional encoding organized around a single correspondence between the two clouds.

A differentiable optimal transport layer first identifies that correspondence, which is then used to normalize points for position encoding. The approach addresses reference-frame differences and learns spatial consistency to reduce ambiguity in features. Correspondence estimation and positional encoding are jointly refined through an iterative procedure, so the two processes can improve together.

The method also progressively aligns the clouds and learns features to refine the rigid transformation. Its positional encoding adds only a small amount of memory and computation. Experiments in indoor and outdoor scenes show performance competitive with state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is therefore an efficient way to make position information useful during alignment, combined with a refinement process that links geometry and feature learning.
neurips-2022-one-inlier-is-first-towards.tldr: A single-correspondence positional encoding supports iterative point-cloud alignment with small overhead and competitive indoor and outdoor performance.

paragraphs: Quadrature approximates an integral using a weighted collection of function evaluations. This paper studies kernel quadrature with convex weights: nonnegative weights that sum to one. The aim is to construct a compact weighted rule that retains a small worst-case integration error while using limited kinds of access to the underlying probability measure.

The construction combines spectral properties of the kernel with recombination results for point measures. These ingredients support selecting and reweighting sampled points to form the quadrature rule. The algorithms require only independent, identically distributed samples from the measure and evaluations of the kernel, making those operations the stated interface to the integration problem.

The paper provides theoretical results supporting small worst-case error and evaluates the construction experimentally. In well-known examples, the experiments indicate that its performance can compete with optimal bounds. That comparison is an empirical finding for the tested examples, rather than a universal claim of optimality. The central contribution is an algorithmic route to sample-based quadrature that preserves convex weights while controlling approximation error.
neurips-2022-positively-weighted-kernel-.tldr: Kernel spectral information and point recombination produce convex-weight quadrature rules from samples, with small worst-case error and promising empirical performance.

paragraphs: Federated min-max learning distributes an optimization problem with competing minimization and maximization objectives across clients. Communication is a major cost, so performing several local updates between exchanges is attractive. Its theoretical benefits are harder to establish here, especially when clients have different data distributions and only some participate in each round.

SAGDA addresses this problem by building control variates from stochastic gradient estimates collected from randomly sampled clients. These serve as correction information within the updates. The framework also uses two learning rates on the server and client sides. Its analysis shows linear speedup with both the number of clients and the number of local update steps.

These results yield an O(epsilon^-2) communication bound, substantially improving the stated state of the art. The framework also reveals standard federated stochastic gradient descent ascent as a special case without control variates, giving the same order of communication complexity for that method. The contribution thus includes both an algorithmic framework and a stronger theoretical understanding of an existing approach.
neurips-2022-sagda-achieving-mathcal-o-e.tldr: SAGDA establishes O(epsilon^-2) communication complexity for federated min-max learning and extends that result to standard FSGDA.

paragraphs: Gaussian homotopy tackles a nonconvex objective by starting with an almost convex version and gradually changing it back toward the original problem. A parameter controls this progression. Existing methods repeatedly solve an optimization problem whenever that parameter changes, creating an expensive loop of inner solves within an outer schedule.

The proposed single-loop framework updates the optimization variables and the homotopy parameter together. This removes the need to complete a separate stationary-point search at every parameter update. The authors analyze computational complexity for deterministic and stochastic settings, considering access either to gradients or to gradient-free information about the homotopy function.

With an appropriately tuned hyperparameter, the convergence rate matches that of gradient descent even though the objective changes during optimization. Numerical experiments show faster convergence than an existing double-loop homotopy method and better solutions than gradient-descent-based methods. The theoretical rate and empirical solution quality answer different questions: the method maintains favorable convergence behavior while retaining the practical motivation for gradually transforming a difficult objective.
neurips-2022-single-loop-gaussian-homoto.tldr: Updating the homotopy parameter and optimization variables together reduces nested computation while matching gradient-descent convergence rates with suitable tuning.

paragraphs: Keypoints summarize useful locations in a 3D shape and can help with reconstruction or alignment. SNAKE investigates the reverse relationship: whether learning to reconstruct a shape can improve keypoint detection. It introduces an unsupervised formulation that couples these tasks instead of treating the point selection problem separately from shape understanding.

The network takes 3D coordinates as input and predicts both implicit shape indicators and keypoint saliency. Sharing this coordinate-based field naturally links where keypoints should appear with the underlying shape. This gives the detector access to shape structure through its learning objective without requiring human semantic keypoint annotations.

The authors report superior performance on object, mesh, and scene benchmarks, including ModelNet40, KeypointNet, SMPL, 3DMatch, and Redwood. Detected keypoints agree with human semantic annotations despite the absence of that supervision. They also show stronger repeatability, particularly after point-cloud downsampling, and enable accurate geometric registration, notably in zero-shot evaluation. These results support shape reconstruction as a useful source of information for learning stable and meaningful keypoints.
neurips-2022-snake-shape-aware-neural-3d.tldr: SNAKE jointly learns shape structure and keypoint saliency without supervision, producing repeatable 3D keypoints that support accurate registration.

paragraphs: Optimal transport describes efficient ways to map one probability distribution onto another. Many applications involve related transport problems whose differences are explained by context, such as the treatment applied to a cell population. CondOT learns across these problems, using context-labeled pairs of input and output distributions.

The method trains a global, context-conditioned map rather than estimating each transport problem in isolation. It aims to fit the observed distribution pairs and produce meaningful maps for previously unseen contexts. Its architecture uses partially input convex neural networks, with a new initialization strategy inspired by Gaussian approximations that the authors describe as robust and efficient.

The demonstrated application predicts how single cells respond to combinations of genetic or therapeutic perturbations. CondOT infers combined effects using observations of the individual perturbations alone. This illustrates the value of sharing information across contextual transport problems: the learned family of maps can support predictions beyond the contexts directly observed during training. The stated generalization goal is supported by this application, rather than presented as a universal guarantee for arbitrary unseen contexts.
neurips-2022-supervised-training-of-cond.tldr: CondOT learns context-conditioned transport maps and demonstrates prediction of combined cellular perturbations from observations of their individual effects.

paragraphs: Distillation with unlabeled data trains a large teacher on available labels, uses it to label additional examples, and then trains a smaller student for deployment. This makes abundant unlabeled data useful when labeled examples are scarce. However, errors in the teacher's generated labels can mislead the student during training.

The paper proposes a principled reweighting of the student's loss to address that problem. The weights are designed as a debiasing correction for the distillation setting, changing how training examples contribute to the learning objective. The method is described as hyperparameter-free, data-agnostic, and simple to implement, so its contribution centers on modifying the student's training loss.

Experiments on popular academic datasets show significant improvements. A theoretical analysis also rigorously supports the method's performance in certain settings. The qualification matters: the theory provides justification within its covered cases, while the experiments supply broader practical evidence on the evaluated datasets. Together, these results support treating the reliability of teacher-generated supervision as part of the student's optimization problem.
neurips-2022-weighted-distillation-with-.tldr: A hyperparameter-free reweighting of the student loss addresses bias from teacher-generated labels and improves distillation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Group invariant learning tries to find reliable predictive mechanisms by dividing training data into inferred groups when environment labels are unavailable. Majority and minority splits have shown empirical promise. This paper asks whether such grouping actually prevents a classifier from using spurious correlations that may change outside the training distribution.

The authors introduce two criteria for assessing that sufficiency. Through theory and experiments, they show that existing methods can violate both criteria and consequently fail when spurious correlations shift. The finding identifies a gap between encouraging performance on some datasets and establishing that a grouping strategy removes reliance on unstable associations.

Their proposed method uses statistical independence tests to construct groups and reweights examples according to group label proportions to meet the criteria. Experiments on synthetic and real data show significant improvements over existing group invariant methods under spurious-correlation shifts. The contribution connects a diagnosis with a remedy: it examines why inferred groups can be inadequate and uses that analysis to guide both group construction and sample weighting.
neurips-2022-when-does-group-invariant-l.tldr: Criteria for resisting spurious correlations motivate independence-based grouping and sample reweighting that improve generalization under tested correlation shifts.
